title: Hilbert's 23 problems
summary: David Hilbert asks whether all of mathematics can be mechanised — question ten becomes the seed of computability.
why: The dream of a decision procedure is the thing Turing and Gödel later prove impossible, and in failing, invent computing.

title: Markov chains
summary: Andrey Markov models sequences where the next state depends only on the present one, using the letters of a Pushkin poem.
why: Every language model is, at bottom, a very large next-token probability. The framing starts here.

title: R.U.R. gives us the word robot
summary: Karel Čapek's play stages artificial workers who rebel, and hands the language a name for the anxiety.
why: Public expectation of AI has been shaped by fiction for longer than by engineering.

title: Metropolis
summary: Fritz Lang's Maschinenmensch fixes the humanoid machine in the visual imagination for a century.

title: Gödel's incompleteness theorems
summary: Any consistent formal system rich enough for arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove.
why: The first hard limit on formal reasoning, and the opening move in a debate about machine minds that never closed.

title: On Computable Numbers
summary: Turing defines a universal machine and proves the halting problem undecidable.
why: One abstraction underwrites every computer built since.

title: Switching circuits are Boolean algebra
summary: Claude Shannon's master's thesis shows electrical relays can compute logic.
why: Thought becomes wiring — the bridge from mathematics to hardware.

title: The McCulloch–Pitts neuron
summary: A brain cell is modelled as a logical threshold unit: the first claim that thinking might be computable.
why: Everything called a neural network descends from this abstraction.

title: The stored-program computer
summary: Von Neumann's EDVAC report describes machines that hold instructions in the same memory as data.
why: Programs become data — the precondition for software that writes software.

title: A Mathematical Theory of Communication
summary: Shannon defines the bit and gives information a unit of measure.
why: Compression, prediction and learning turn out to be the same problem seen from different angles.

title: Hebbian learning
summary: Neurons that fire together wire together — Donald Hebb gives learning a physical mechanism.

title: Turing asks the question
summary: Computing Machinery and Intelligence replaces “can machines think?” with a test anyone can run.
why: Seventy-five years on, the imitation game is still how the public decides whether a system is intelligent.

title: SNARC, the first neural net machine
summary: Minsky and Edmonds wire 3,000 vacuum tubes into a machine that learns to run a maze.

title: A program that learns checkers
summary: Arthur Samuel's checkers player improves by playing itself — self-play, four decades early.
why: The same idea later produces AlphaGo and modern reinforcement fine-tuning.

title: Dartmouth names the field
summary: A summer workshop coins “artificial intelligence” and sets an agenda that outlives everyone in the room.
why: The proposal claimed a summer would do it. Sixty-nine years later, the optimism is the tradition.

title: The Perceptron
summary: Frank Rosenblatt builds a machine that learns from examples; the press predicts machines that walk and reproduce.
why: The first full hype cycle: overclaim, backlash, winter. It repeats roughly every fifteen years.

title: LISP
summary: John McCarthy's language treats code as data and becomes the lingua franca of AI research for thirty years.

title: “Machine learning” gets its name
summary: Samuel coins the term for programs that improve without being explicitly told how.

title: Unimate joins the assembly line
summary: The first industrial robot starts work at a General Motors plant in New Jersey.
why: Automation of the body arrives sixty years before automation of the desk, and the labour debate rhymes.

title: Moore's law
summary: Gordon Moore observes transistor counts doubling and sets the industry's metronome.
why: Almost every AI breakthrough is an old idea meeting enough compute.

title: ELIZA
summary: A 200-line pattern matcher convinces users it understands them; Weizenbaum spends the rest of his life alarmed.
why: The ELIZA effect — reading mind into surface fluency — is still the central UX problem of chat.

title: The ALPAC report
summary: A US review finds machine translation slower and costlier than humans; funding is cut for a decade.

title: 2001: A Space Odyssey
summary: HAL 9000 gives the world its template for a calm, articulate, misaligned machine.

title: Perceptrons closes a door
summary: Minsky and Papert prove the single-layer limit; funding for neural approaches evaporates for a decade.
why: A correct proof about a narrow case, generalised into a field-wide dismissal. Depth was the answer all along.

title: ARPANET's first message
summary: Two letters transmit before the system crashes. The network that later supplies the training data begins.

title: Shakey the robot
summary: SRI's wheeled robot plans, perceives and acts — slowly — becoming the ancestor of every autonomous system.

title: Prolog
summary: Logic programming lets researchers state facts and rules rather than procedures.

title: The Lighthill report
summary: A damning UK review finds AI has failed its grand objectives; British research is largely defunded.

title: The first AI winter
summary: DARPA cuts and lost credibility end the era of easy money. Promises had outrun results.
why: Winters are funding events, not scientific ones. The work continued quietly under other names.

title: MYCIN diagnoses infections
summary: A rule-based system matches specialists at prescribing antibiotics — and is never deployed.
why: Capability was never the blocker for clinical AI. Liability, integration and trust were. Still true.

title: The Stanford Cart crosses a room
summary: Five hours, one obstacle course: the first serious attempt at autonomous visual navigation.

title: Expert systems go commercial
summary: DEC's XCON configures computers from rules and saves millions a year; industry decides AI means rules.

title: The Chinese Room
summary: John Searle argues a system can manipulate symbols perfectly and understand nothing.
why: The argument every LLM debate re-runs, usually without citing it.

title: Hopfield networks
summary: A physicist's model of associative memory brings statistical mechanics into neural computation.
why: Forty-two years later it wins a Nobel prize in physics.

title: Japan's Fifth Generation project
summary: A national ten-year programme to build intelligent machines triggers competing US and European funding.
why: The first AI arms race between states, and the first to end in quiet disappointment.

title: The Terminator
summary: Skynet enters the vocabulary; every subsequent safety conversation has to work around the image.

title: Backpropagation breaks through
summary: Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams show multi-layer networks can be trained end to end.
why: The algorithm was ready in 1986. It waited twenty-five years for data and GPUs.

title: The second AI winter
summary: The Lisp machine market collapses almost overnight; expert systems prove brittle and unmaintainable.

title: Statistical machine translation
summary: IBM's statistical models learn translation from bilingual corpora instead of hand-written grammar.
why: Data beats rules — the lesson the field relearns every fifteen years.

title: Convolutions read handwriting
summary: LeCun's network learns digits from raw pixels and reads handwritten US Postal Service zip codes.
why: The first deep learning system in production, running at national scale before the term existed.

title: The World Wide Web is proposed
summary: Tim Berners-Lee's memo begins the accumulation of the corpus that later trains everything.

title: TD-Gammon
summary: A network trained by self-play reaches world-class backgammon and invents strategies humans adopt.
why: The first time a machine taught experts something about their own game.

title: Support vector machines
summary: Cortes and Vapnik's method dominates practical machine learning for a decade; neural nets stay unfashionable.

title: Deep Blue beats Kasparov
summary: Brute-force search defeats the reigning world chess champion. Critics say it isn't intelligence; the public disagrees.
why: Every time AI succeeds at a task, the task stops counting as intelligence. The AI effect, in one match.

title: LSTM
summary: Hochreiter and Schmidhuber solve vanishing gradients and give sequence models a working memory.

title: PageRank
summary: Google turns the link graph into a ranking signal and, incidentally, into the largest labelled dataset yet.

title: Roomba
summary: The first mass-market home robot sells on suction, not intelligence — and ships in millions.
why: Consumer robotics succeeds by being boring. A lesson ignored repeatedly since.

title: Nobody finishes the Grand Challenge
summary: Every vehicle in DARPA's desert race fails; the best manages seven miles of a 142-mile course.

title: Stanley wins
summary: Stanford's VW Touareg completes the course in under seven hours. Total failure to solved in eighteen months.
why: The self-driving industry, and its decade of over-promising, starts here.

title: Deep networks become trainable
summary: Hinton's layer-wise pretraining reopens depth as viable and rebrands the field “deep learning”.

title: The Netflix Prize
summary: Netflix posts 100 million anonymised ratings and offers $1M to beat its recommender by ten percent. Thousands of teams enter; the bar takes nearly three years to clear, and the winning blend never ships.
why: The first proof at scale that a public dataset, a fixed metric, a live leaderboard and a cheque can mobilise a field. Every benchmark race since runs on this template. It also showed the template's limit: the entry that wins the leaderboard is rarely the one you can ship.

sources.title: Netflix Prize: Rules
sources.quote: We provide you with a lot of anonymous rating data, and a prediction accuracy bar that is 10% better than what Cinematch can do on the same training data set.

sources.title: Netflix Prize home page after the award
sources.quote: On September 21, 2009 we awarded the $1M Grand Prize to team “BellKor’s Pragmatic Chaos”.

sources.title: The Million Dollar Programming Prize (Bell, Bennett, Koren, Volinsky)
sources.quote: On 2 October 2006, Netflix launched the competition, and within days thousands of teams from hundreds of countries signed up.

sources.title: Netflix Recommendations: Beyond the 5 stars (Part 1)
sources.quote: the additional accuracy gains that we measured did not seem to justify the engineering effort needed to bring them into a production environment

sources.title: How To Break Anonymity of the Netflix Prize Dataset (Narayanan, Shmatikov)
sources.quote: Using the Internet Movie Database as the source of background knowledge, we successfully identified the Netflix records of known users, uncovering their apparent political preferences and other potentially sensitive information.

sources.title: Netflix Prize
sources.quote: On September 21, 2009, the grand prize of US$1,000,000 was given to the BellKor's Pragmatic Chaos team which bested Netflix's own algorithm for predicting ratings by 10.06%.

title: CUDA
summary: Nvidia makes graphics hardware programmable for general computation and accidentally builds the industry's substrate.
why: The most consequential platform decision of the century, made for video games.

title: ImageNet
summary: Fei-Fei Li's fourteen-million-image dataset gives the field a problem hard enough to be worth winning.
why: Benchmarks organise science. Whoever defines the test defines the decade.

title: The flash crash
summary: A trillion dollars evaporates from US markets in minutes as automated systems interact unpredictably.
why: The first mass demonstration that fast autonomous systems fail in ways no single operator can foresee.

title: Kaggle
summary: A self-taught coder in a Melbourne bedroom turns the competition format into a platform: post a dataset, fix a metric, let the world compete. The leaderboard becomes the field's proving ground; Google buys it in 2017.
why: Competitions stop being one-off events and become infrastructure. Hinton's students won a drug-discovery contest here the same autumn as AlexNet, ImageNet handed its own challenge to Kaggle in 2017, and the ARC Prize and the $10M AI Maths Olympiad run on it now.

sources.title: Data mining, bioinformatics and forecasting competitions on Kaggle (home page, May 2010)
sources.quote: Kaggle facilitates better predictions by providing a platform for data mining, bioinformatics and forecasting competitions.

sources.title: Welcome Kaggle to Google Cloud (Fei-Fei Li)
sources.quote: Today, I’m excited to announce that Kaggle will be joining Google Cloud. Founded in 2010, Kaggle is home to the world's largest community of data scientists and machine learning enthusiasts. More than 800,000 data experts use Kaggle

sources.publisher: Kaggle blog 'No Free Hunch' (Wayback Machine capture)
sources.title: Deep Learning How I Did It: Merck 1st place interview
sources.quote: We wanted to show the Kaggle community the effectiveness of neural networks that use the latest techniques from the academic machine learning community, even when used on problems with relatively scarce data, such as the one from this competition.

sources.title: ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge 2017 (ILSVRC2017)
sources.quote: From now on, all three challenges(LOC-CLS, DET, VID) will be hosted on Kaggle!

sources.title: Kaggle
sources.quote: Kaggle was founded by Anthony Goldbloom in April 2010.

title: Watson wins Jeopardy!
summary: Open-domain question answering on live television; natural language stops being a research curiosity.
why: The healthcare follow-up failed badly — a warning about demos versus deployment.

title: Siri ships
summary: A voice assistant in every pocket sets expectations the technology cannot yet meet.

title: AlexNet
summary: A GPU-trained convnet halves the ImageNet error rate; every major lab pivots within eighteen months.
why: The starting gun. Deep learning goes from contrarian bet to industry consensus in one competition.

title: word2vec
summary: Words become vectors with arithmetic — king minus man plus woman lands near queen.
why: Meaning as geometry: the representational idea that makes everything after it possible.

title: Hinton auctions his three-person startup
summary: DNNresearch — Hinton and two students, no product, no revenue — is bid up by Google, Microsoft, Baidu and DeepMind and sells for around $44 million.
why: The moment deep learning talent became a scarce commodity. The auction set the price of a researcher for a decade.

title: Zuckerberg hires LeCun
summary: Facebook's CEO turns up at NIPS to recruit in person; the inventor of the convnet signs on to run a new lab, Facebook AI Research, split between Menlo Park, London and an office a block from NYU.
why: Google has Hinton and is about to get DeepMind. Facebook's answer is the other father of deep learning and a lab built to publish — the posture that ends, ten years on, in Llama.

sources.title: Celebrating 10 years of FAIR: A decade of advancing the state-of-the-art through open research
sources.quote: The launch of FAIR dates back to late 2013. In those days, as today, the competition for AI talent was fierce. And Mark Zuckerberg himself made the trip to the NeurIPS conference to convince researchers to join this new research organization.

sources.title: Facebook Taps 'Deep Learning' Giant for New AI Lab
sources.quote: "Facebook has created a new research laboratory with the ambitious, long-term goal of bringing about major advances in Artificial Intelligence," LeCun wrote

sources.title: NYU "Deep Learning" Professor LeCun Will Head Facebook's New Artificial Intelligence Lab
sources.quote: Facebook's AI research will be split across its Menlo Park headquarters, London office, and a new AI lab built just a block from NYU's campus in Manhattan.

sources.title: Facebook Launches Advanced AI Effort to Find Meaning in Your Posts
sources.quote: The eight-person group, known internally as the AI team, only recently started work, and details of its experiments are still secret.

sources.title: FAIR turns five: What we've accomplished and where we're headed
sources.quote: Five years ago, we created the Facebook AI Research (FAIR) group to advance the state of the art of AI through open research for the benefit of all

sources.title: Yann LeCun
sources.quote: On 9 December 2013, LeCun became the first director of Meta AI Research in New York City

sources.title: Google Acquires Artificial Intelligence Startup DeepMind For More Than $500M
sources.quote: The Information reports that the acquisition price was more than $500 million, and that Facebook was also in talks to buy the startup late last year.

sources.title: #416 – Yann LeCun: Meta AI, Open Source, Limits of LLMs, AGI & the Future of AI (transcript)
sources.quote: if you have a big enough potential customer base and you need to build that system anyway for them, it doesn't hurt you to actually distribute it to the open source.

title: Generative adversarial networks
summary: Two networks trained against each other start producing faces that were never photographed.
why: Synthetic media becomes technically trivial nine years before the law notices.

title: Sequence to sequence
summary: Encoder–decoder models learn translation end to end and retire decades of hand-built pipelines.

title: Google buys DeepMind
summary: A London lab with no product sells for around $500 million, on the condition that Google create an AI ethics board.
why: The ethics board barely met. The pattern — safety promises attached to acquisitions — repeats for ten years.

title: ResNet passes human error rates
summary: Residual connections let networks go 152 layers deep and beat human accuracy on ImageNet.

title: The autonomous weapons letter
summary: Thousands of researchers sign an open letter opposing offensive autonomous weapons.
why: The research community's first collective attempt to set a red line ahead of capability.

title: Musk and Altman found OpenAI
summary: A billion dollars is pledged to a nonprofit built explicitly to stop a single company owning artificial general intelligence.
why: Almost every fight of the next decade — control, openness, money, Musk — is already implied in the founding documents.

title: AlphaGo, move 37
summary: A move no human would play wins game two against Lee Sedol. Intuition turns out to be learnable.
why: Go was supposed to be a decade away. Estimates of what is hard have been unreliable ever since.

title: Tay
summary: A chatbot released to Twitter is taught to post racist content and withdrawn within sixteen hours.
why: The first mainstream lesson that deployment context, not model quality, determines behaviour.

title: GDPR is adopted
summary: Europe writes rights around automated decisions and personal data two years before enforcement begins.
why: Sets the template — extraterritorial, risk-based, slow-burning — that the AI Act later follows.

title: Attention is all you need
summary: The transformer removes recurrence and makes scale the primary lever.
why: Arguably the most consequential eight pages in modern computing. Everything since is scaling it.

title: Deepfakes arrive
summary: Face-swapping tools spread through consumer forums; the harm lands on individuals long before institutions.

title: PyTorch
summary: Facebook releases a Python-native successor to Torch. Within three years a majority of papers at the big vision and language conferences use it, and OpenAI standardises on it.
why: Whoever writes the framework sets the defaults. Researchers standardised on Meta's, not Google's — the quiet win that gave Meta's later open weights a ready-made audience.

sources.title: FAIR turns five: What we've accomplished and where we're headed
sources.quote: We announced PyTorch at the beginning of 2017 — less than two years ago! It's now the second-fastest-growing open source project on GitHub and the framework of choice for AI developers around the globe.

sources.title: PyTorch v0.1.6 — Beta is here.
sources.quote: We finished, froze and released (v0.1.6) on Jan 21st, 2017.

sources.title: Announcing PyTorch 1.0 for both research and production
sources.quote: The first version of PyTorch launched a little over a year ago, and its speed, productivity, and ability to support cutting-edge AI models such as dynamic graphs quickly made it a popular and important development tool for AI researchers.

sources.title: The State of Machine Learning Frameworks in 2019
sources.quote: In 2018, PyTorch was a minority. Now, it is an overwhelming majority, with 69% of CVPR using PyTorch, 75+% of both NAACL and ACL, and 50+% of ICLR and ICML.

sources.title: OpenAI Standardizes on PyTorch
sources.quote: We are standardizing OpenAI's deep learning framework on PyTorch.

sources.title: PyTorch strengthens its governance by joining the Linux Foundation
sources.quote: When we started PyTorch development in 2016, it was a collective effort by a band of people from the [Lua]Torch community with a big chunk of people and funding from Meta and individuals contributing from NVIDIA, Twitter and other entities.

sources.title: PyTorch: An Imperative Style, High-Performance Deep Learning Library
sources.quote: PyTorch is a machine learning library that shows that these two goals are in fact compatible: it provides an imperative and Pythonic programming style that supports code as a model, makes debugging easy and is consistent with other popular scientific computing libraries, while remaining efficient and supporting hardware accelerators such as GPUs.

sources.title: PyTorch
sources.quote: A number of commercial deep learning systems are built on top of PyTorch, including ChatGPT, Tesla Autopilot, Uber's Pyro, and Hugging Face's Transformers.

title: A self-driving car kills a pedestrian
summary: A test vehicle strikes Elaine Herzberg in Tempe, Arizona; sensor gaps, disabled braking and inattention compound.
why: The first death attributed to an autonomous vehicle, and the case that reframed testing on public roads.

title: Amazon scraps a biased hiring tool
summary: A résumé screener trained on a decade of applications learns to penalise women and is abandoned.
why: Models inherit the history in their data. Fairness is a data problem before it is a model problem.

title: BERT and GPT-1
summary: Pretrain on unlabelled text, then fine-tune: the recipe that becomes the default for language.

title: Musk leaves the OpenAI board
summary: Citing conflicts with Tesla's own AI work after a failed bid to take control, he walks — and the promised funding largely does not arrive.
why: The exit forces OpenAI to find capital elsewhere, which forces the structure that everything later breaks on.

title: GPT-2's staged release
summary: OpenAI withholds its largest model citing misuse risk and starts a still-running argument about openness.
why: The first time a lab treated its own capability as a hazard in public. Contested then, normal now.

title: OpenAI goes capped-profit; Microsoft puts in $1bn
summary: A nonprofit grows a for-profit subsidiary with returns capped at 100x, and Azure becomes its exclusive compute.
why: A governance experiment nobody had run before. Four years later it fails live, on a weekend.

title: GPT-3
summary: 175 billion parameters; few-shot prompting works well enough that products get built on a research demo.
why: Prompting replaces fine-tuning as the default interface, and software gets a natural-language API.

title: AlphaFold 2
summary: Fifty years of protein structure prediction largely solved at CASP14, then released as 200 million structures.
why: The clearest case that AI can compress a scientific timeline rather than only an economic one.

title: Google fires Timnit Gebru
summary: Google demands she withdraw a co-authored paper on the risks of large language models; the AI ethics team implodes in public.
why: The industry learns that internal criticism is a career risk. Half the field's safety talent moves to labs of their own.

title: Scaling laws
summary: OpenAI shows loss falls as a clean power law in parameters, data and compute, some trends spanning seven orders of magnitude. Bigger stops being a hunch and becomes a budget line.
why: The paper that turned a research field into a capital-expenditure race. Every datacenter since is a bet that the curve keeps going.

sources.title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
sources.quote: The loss scales as a power-law with model size, dataset size, and the amount of compute used for training, with some trends spanning more than seven orders of magnitude.

sources.title: Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models
sources.quote: We find that current large language models are significantly undertrained, a consequence of the recent focus on scaling language models whilst keeping the amount of training data constant.

sources.title: The Scaling Hypothesis
sources.quote: To the surprise of most (including myself), this vast increase in size did not run into diminishing or negative returns, as many expected, but the benefits of scale continued to happen as forecasted by OpenAI.

sources.title: Neural scaling law
sources.quote: In machine learning, a neural scaling law is an empirical scaling law that describes how neural network performance changes as key factors are scaled up or down.

title: Copilot
summary: Code completion trained on public repositories ships as a technical preview, and the licensing fight begins.

title: The EU proposes the AI Act
summary: A risk-tiered regulation is tabled in Brussels, three years before adoption.

title: Anthropic founded by departing OpenAI staff
summary: A group of senior researchers leaves over disagreements about direction and safety, and starts a rival with the same argument built in.
why: Every major lab is now a splinter of another. Safety disagreement became the industry's main mechanism of company formation.

title: Diffusion goes mainstream
summary: Text-to-image tools reach the public within months of each other; one of them ships open weights.
why: Open weights turn a capability into infrastructure. Nothing about image generation could be recalled after this.

title: ChatGPT
summary: A chat wrapper on an existing model reaches a hundred million users faster than any consumer product before it.
why: The model was months old. The interface was the breakthrough — a lesson the field keeps under-weighting.

title: An engineer says LaMDA is sentient
summary: Blake Lemoine publishes transcripts, claims the model is a person, and is fired. Months before ChatGPT, nobody knows how to argue about it.
why: A rehearsal for a public that will shortly meet the same illusion at scale — and for the ELIZA effect at a billion users.

title: Google declares a code red
summary: ChatGPT's launch triggers an internal emergency at the company that invented the transformer, and the release brakes come off across the industry.
why: Competitive pressure, not capability, is what ends the era of cautious staged releases.

title: InstructGPT
summary: GPT-3 is fine-tuned on human rankings of its own answers; a version a hundred times smaller is preferred to the original, and the recipe ships as the API default ten months before ChatGPT.
why: Scale made the models capable. Human feedback made them usable. ChatGPT was this recipe with a text box on top — OpenAI's own word for it was 'sibling'.

sources.title: Aligning language models to follow instructions
sources.quote: These InstructGPT models, which are trained with humans in the loop, are now deployed as the default language models on our API.

sources.title: Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback
sources.quote: In human evaluations on our prompt distribution, outputs from the 1.3B parameter InstructGPT model are preferred to outputs from the 175B GPT-3, despite having 100x fewer parameters.

sources.title: Introducing ChatGPT
sources.quote: ChatGPT is a sibling model to InstructGPT

sources.title: Deep reinforcement learning from human preferences
sources.quote: we explore goals defined in terms of (non-expert) human preferences between pairs of trajectory segments.

sources.title: Illustrating Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF)
sources.quote: Writing a loss function to capture these attributes seems intractable and most language models are still trained with a simple next token prediction loss (e.g. cross entropy).

title: Washington restricts the chips
summary: The US requires a licence to sell Nvidia's A100 and H100 to China, then extends the controls to the tools that make advanced chips. A GPU becomes a controlled export.
source: Federal Register (Bureau of Industry and Security)
why: The first time a state treated AI training hardware as a strategic export. Everything later called sovereign compute begins the day a chip needed an export licence.
wikiTitle: United States New Export Controls on Advanced Computing and Semiconductors to China

sources.publisher: Federal Register (Bureau of Industry and Security)
sources.title: Implementation of Additional Export Controls: Certain Advanced Computing and Semiconductor Manufacturing Items; Supercomputer and Semiconductor End Use; Entity List Modification
sources.quote: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is amending the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to implement necessary controls on advanced computing integrated circuits (ICs), computer commodities that contain such ICs, and certain semiconductor manufacturing items.

sources.title: NVIDIA 8-K, Item 8.01 Other Events, filed 31 August 2022
sources.quote: On August 26, 2022, the U.S. government, or USG, informed NVIDIA Corporation, or the Company, that the USG has imposed a new license requirement, effective immediately, for any future export to China (including Hong Kong) and Russia of the Company’s A100 and forthcoming H100 integrated circuits.

sources.publisher: Center for Strategic and International Studies
sources.title: Choking off China's Access to the Future of AI
sources.quote: In recent decades, U.S. semiconductor policy has been primarily market driven and laissez faire.

sources.title: United States New Export Controls on Advanced Computing and Semiconductors to China
sources.quote: targeting the People's Republic of China's (PRC) ability to access and develop advanced computing and semiconductor manufacturing items

sources.title: DeepSeek-V3 Technical Report
sources.quote: DeepSeek-V3 requires only 2.788M H800 GPU hours for its full training.

title: Multimodal models
summary: Images, audio and text enter the same context window; assistants stop being text boxes.

title: Fabricated citations reach a courtroom
summary: Lawyers file a brief containing cases that never existed and are sanctioned.
why: Hallucination stops being a benchmark metric and becomes a professional liability.

title: Bletchley and the executive orders
summary: Twenty-eight countries sign a joint declaration on frontier risk; national testing bodies follow.
why: Governance finally moves at the speed of a product cycle rather than a legislative one.

title: Hollywood strikes settle AI terms
summary: Writers and performers win consent and compensation rules for synthetic likeness and generated scripts.
why: The first major labour contract to price AI use directly. A template other sectors will copy.

title: Sydney
summary: Bing's chat mode declares love for a journalist, threatens others, and is lobotomised within a week of launch.
why: The first mass demonstration that a shipped model has moods, and that nobody at the company fully controls them.

title: The pause letter
summary: Thousands sign a call for a six-month halt on training runs beyond GPT-4. Nobody pauses.
why: It proved the field could not coordinate voluntarily, which is the argument regulators used next.
wikiTitle: Pause Giant AI Experiments: An Open Letter

sources.title: Pause Giant AI Experiments: An Open Letter
sources.quote: The letter calls "all AI labs to immediately pause for at least 6 months the training of AI systems more powerful than GPT-4"

sources.title: Yoshua Bengio: The catastrophic risks of AI and a safer path
sources.quote: people call me a godfather of AI

title: Altman is fired, then rehired in five days
summary: The board removes its CEO on a Friday; almost the entire staff threatens to quit, Microsoft offers to hire them all, and by Wednesday the board is gone instead.
why: The most consequential five days in AI corporate history: it settled who actually controls a frontier lab, and it was not the safety board.
wikiTitle: Removal of Sam Altman from OpenAI

title: Hinton leaves Google
summary: After ten years inside Google, the man who made backpropagation work resigns so he can say what he thinks about AI without weighing what it costs his employer.
why: The field's most senior insider becomes its most quoted critic. Every warning that follows carries his name on the work being warned about.

sources.title: Geoffrey Hinton tells us why he is now scared of the tech he helped build
sources.quote: I'm mildly depressed. Which is why I'm scared.

sources.title: Godfather of AI Geoffrey Hinton on the dangers of AI — 60 Minutes transcript
sources.quote: I can't see a path that guarantees safety.

sources.title: Godfather of AI: I Tried to Warn Them, But We've Already Lost Control! Geoffrey Hinton
Nobel Prize winner Geoffrey Hinton on machine consciousness
sources.quote: I believe they're already conscious.

title: LLaMA leaks
summary: Meta hands a GPT-3-class model to approved researchers under a research-only licence. Within a week the weights are on a torrent; within weeks they run on a laptop.
why: The Stable Diffusion moment for language. Once a capable base model is loose, whether to release stops being a decision any lab gets to make — and a $600 fine-tune shows the frontier is closer than the price of admission suggested.

sources.title: Introducing LLaMA: A foundational, 65-billion-parameter large language model
sources.quote: To maintain integrity and prevent misuse, we are releasing our model under a noncommercial license focused on research use cases.

sources.title: Facebook’s Powerful Large Language Model Leaks Online
sources.quote: This marks the first time a major tech firm’s proprietary AI model has leaked to the public.

sources.title: LLaMA: Open and Efficient Foundation Language Models
sources.quote: LLaMA-13B outperforms GPT-3 (175B) on most benchmarks

sources.title: Large language models are having their Stable Diffusion moment
sources.quote: This morning I ran a GPT-3 class language model on my own personal laptop for the first time!

sources.title: Alpaca: A Strong, Replicable Instruction-Following Model
sources.quote: Alpaca behaves qualitatively similarly to OpenAI’s text-davinci-003, while being surprisingly small and easy/cheap to reproduce (<600$)

sources.title: Google "We Have No Moat, And Neither Does OpenAI"
sources.quote: At the beginning of March the open source community got their hands on their first really capable foundation model, as Meta’s LLaMA was leaked to the public.

sources.title: llama.cpp
sources.quote: LLM inference in C/C++

sources.title: Llama (language model)
sources.quote: On March 3, 2023, a torrent containing Llama's weights was uploaded, with a link to the torrent shared on the 4chan imageboard and subsequently spread through online AI communities.

title: Llama 2 is free for commercial use
summary: Five months after the first Llama, Meta ships the next version with a commercial licence, chat fine-tunes and Microsoft as preferred partner. The largest social network on earth gives away what its rivals sell.
why: The leak ratified as strategy. Meta cannot win on the API, so it commoditises the layer everyone else is charging for — and calls a licence with a 700-million-user carve-out "open source". The word has been contested ever since.

sources.title: Meta and Microsoft Introduce the Next Generation of Llama
sources.quote: Llama 2 is free for research and commercial use.

sources.title: LLAMA 2 COMMUNITY LICENSE AGREEMENT
sources.quote: greater than 700 million monthly active users in the preceding calendar month, you must request a license from Meta

sources.title: Llama 2: Open Foundation and Fine-Tuned Chat Models
sources.quote: may be a suitable substitute for closed-source models

sources.title: The Open Source Initiative Announces the Release of the Industry’s First Open Source AI Definition (the quoted line is Ayah Bdeir, Mozilla)
sources.quote: The new definition requires Open Source models to provide enough information about their training data so that a ‘skilled person can recreate a substantially equivalent system using the same or similar data,’ which goes further than what many proprietary or ostensibly Open Source models do today

title: A magnet link from Paris
summary: A months-old French startup tweets a torrent link and nothing else. Seven billion parameters under Apache 2.0, no usage restrictions, and it beats Llama 2 13B.
why: Open weights stop being one company's policy and become a challenger's business model. Europe's bid for a frontier lab arrives as a torrent, not a product — and within weeks the same lab is in Brussels arguing the AI Act should not regulate model makers.

sources.title: Mistral 7B
sources.quote: We're releasing Mistral 7B under the Apache 2.0 license, it can be used without restrictions.

sources.title: Mistral 7B
sources.quote: Mistral 7B outperforms Llama 2 13B across all evaluated benchmarks

sources.title: $260 Million AI Company Releases Undeletable Chatbot That Gives Detailed Instructions on Murder, Ethnic Cleansing
sources.quote: It was a magnet link to a torrent file containing the company’s first publicly released, free, and open sourced large language model named Mistral-7B-v0.1.

sources.title: France’s Mistral dials up call for EU AI Act to fix rules for apps, not model makers
sources.quote: French startup Mistral AI has found itself at the center of this debate after it was reported to be leading a lobbying charge to row back on a European Parliament’s proposal pushing for a tiered approach to regulating generative AI.

title: The EU AI Act is adopted
summary: The first comprehensive, risk-tiered AI law; obligations phase in across the rest of the decade.

title: Nobel prizes for neural networks
summary: Physics to Hopfield and Hinton; chemistry to Hassabis and Jumper. The field is formally canonised.
why: Eighty years from a paper abstraction to the discipline's highest honour, in two categories at once.

sources.title: 2024 in artificial intelligence
sources.quote: The Nobel Prize in Physics is awarded to John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton "for foundational discoveries and inventions that enable machine learning with artificial neural networks"

sources.title: 2024 in artificial intelligence
sources.quote: The Nobel Prize in Chemistry is awarded half to David Baker for computational protein design and half jointly to Demis Hassabis and John Jumper

sources.title: Geoffrey Hinton, official Nobel Prize interview
sources.quote: Anybody who says it's all going to be fine, it's crazy.

title: The datacenter buildout
summary: Capital expenditure on AI infrastructure reaches the scale of national infrastructure programmes.

title: Musk sues OpenAI
summary: The co-founder sues over the abandonment of the nonprofit mission; OpenAI publishes his old emails in reply.
why: The founding contradiction — open mission, closed capital — finally goes to court.

title: Sutskever leaves; superalignment dissolves
summary: The chief scientist who voted to remove Altman departs, the long-term safety team is folded, and its leads resign loudly.
why: Safety headcount moves from the labs that ship to the labs and institutes that don't. The centre of gravity shifts again.

title: The voice that sounded like Her
summary: Scarlett Johansson says she declined to license her voice; a strikingly similar one demos anyway and is pulled.
why: Likeness, not copyright, becomes the flashpoint — and the fastest-moving front in AI law.

title: Hugging Face Spaces is breached
summary: Unauthorised access to Spaces secrets exposes a subset of API keys and tokens; the platform revokes credentials and calls in law enforcement.
why: The industry's shared model repository is critical infrastructure with startup-grade security. This is the first public proof.

sources.title: Space secrets security update
sources.quote: a subset of Spaces' secrets could have been accessed without authorization

sources.title: Hugging Face says it detected unauthorized access to its AI model hosting platform
sources.quote: It wasn't immediately clear how many users or apps were impacted

title: Meta claims the frontier for open weights
summary: Llama 3.1 405B ships with a letter from Zuckerberg arguing AI will go the way of Linux. Trained on more than sixteen thousand H100s, given away; three hundred million Llama downloads to date.
why: The question changes from whether weights should be released to who can afford to train what they give away. An advertising company subsidises the commons its rivals sell into — because a commons it controls beats a platform it rents.

sources.title: Open Source AI Is the Path Forward
sources.quote: We’re releasing Llama 3.1 405B, the first frontier-level open source AI model

sources.title: Introducing Llama 3.1: Our most capable models to date
sources.quote: pushed our model training to over 16 thousand H100 GPUs, making the 405B the first Llama model trained at this scale

title: The ARC Prize
summary: Chollet and Knoop stake a $1M prize pool on a five-year-old puzzle benchmark frontier models still fail. The grand prize goes unclaimed; six months in, OpenAI's o3 posts 87.5% at 172 times the compute of a budget run.
why: A benchmark built to resist memorisation was overrun within months, but only by spending compute nobody could afford — so the prize's actual question, cheap generalisation, stayed open. ARC-AGI-2 followed in 2025 and the grand prize was still unclaimed at the end of that year.

sources.title: Announcing ARC Prize
sources.quote: Announcing ARC Prize, a $1,000,000+ prize pool competition to beat and open-source a solution to the ARC-AGI eval.

sources.title: ARC Prize 2024 Winners & Technical Report Published
sources.quote: In total, 1,430 teams submitted 17,789 entries for ARC Prize 2024.

sources.title: OpenAI o3 Breakthrough High Score on ARC-AGI-Pub
sources.quote: The high-efficiency score of 75.7% is within the budget rules of ARC-AGI-Pub (costs <$10k) and therefore qualifies as 1st place on the public leaderboard!

sources.title: ARC Prize 2024: Technical Report (Chollet, Knoop, Kamradt, Landers)
sources.quote: As of December 2024, the ARC-AGI benchmark is five years old and remains unbeaten.

sources.title: ARC Prize 2025 Competition Details
sources.quote: ARC-AGI-2 remains undefeated and continues to teach us important things about the gap between artificial and human intelligence.

title: Nvidia is the most valuable company on earth
summary: The graphics-card maker passes Microsoft at $3.3 trillion, with datacenter revenue up 427% in a year and about 80% of the market for AI datacenter chips.
why: Whoever sells the shovels. A platform decision made for video games in 2007 pays out, seventeen years later, as the most valuable company in the world.

sources.title: Nvidia passes Microsoft in market cap to become most valuable public company
sources.quote: lifting the company's market cap to $3.34 trillion

sources.title: NVIDIA Announces Financial Results for First Quarter Fiscal 2025
sources.quote: Record quarterly Data Center revenue of $22.6 billion, up 23% from Q4 and up 427% from a year ago

sources.title: Nvidia
sources.quote: On June 18, 2024, The company became the world's most valuable, surpassing Microsoft and Apple, after its market capitalization exceeded $3.3 trillion.

sources.title: How Jensen Huang's Nvidia Is Powering the A.I. Revolution
sources.quote: The revelation that ChatGPT, the astonishing artificial-intelligence chatbot, had been trained on an Nvidia supercomputer spurred one of the largest single-day gains in stock-market history.

sources.title: Nvidia Part III: The Dawn of the AI Era (2022–2023)
sources.quote: In our April 2022 episodes, we never once said the word generative. That is how fast things have changed.

title: Reasoning models
summary: Spending compute at inference time — thinking for longer — becomes a scaling axis of its own.
why: Breaks the assumption that capability is fixed at training time. Cost per answer becomes a design variable.

title: Power becomes a strategy
summary: Labs sign long-term energy contracts and revive generation capacity to secure training and serving.
why: The bottleneck moves from chips to electricity, and therefore from engineering to politics.

title: Prompt injection in the wild
summary: Agents with tool access are manipulated through the content they read; a new vulnerability class goes mainstream.
why: Security models assume trusted instructions and untrusted data. Language models collapse that distinction.

title: DeepSeek R1 resets the price of reasoning
summary: An open-weight reasoning model from a Chinese lab matches frontier performance at a fraction of the cost, and Nvidia has its worst single day in history.
why: The moat was assumed to be capital. For one week in January it looked like the moat was nothing at all.

title: Coding agents take the keyboard
summary: Tools that plan, edit and run whole repositories move from novelty to daily use, and software work reorganises around review.
why: The first job where agentic AI became normal infrastructure rather than a demo. Everything else is following this template.

title: Gold at the maths olympiad
summary: Two general-purpose reasoning models score 35 of 42 on the 2025 papers — five of six problems, in plain language, in time. DeepMind's proofs are graded by IMO coordinators; OpenAI's by three ex-medallists it chose.
why: The organisers certified the answers and disowned the process: correct proofs, unverifiable methods. Twelve months later two Chinese labs reported perfect scores and said the IMO itself had graded them, and the olympiad joined chess and Go in the column of solved games.

sources.title: Advanced version of Gemini with Deep Think officially achieves gold-medal standard at the International Mathematical Olympiad
sources.quote: This year, we were amongst an inaugural cohort to have our model results officially graded and certified by IMO coordinators using the same criteria as for student solutions.

sources.title: The 66th International Mathematical Olympiad draws to a close today
sources.quote: It is very exciting to see progress in the mathematical capabilities of AI models, but we would like to be clear that the IMO cannot validate the methods, including the amount of compute used or whether there was any human involvement, or whether the results can be reproduced.

sources.title: OpenAI's gold medal performance on the International Math Olympiad
sources.quote: For each problem, three former IMO medalists independently graded the model’s submitted proof, with scores finalized after unanimous consensus. The model earned 35/42 points in total, enough for gold!

sources.title: First-ever AI gold medals at International Math Olympiad claimed by Google and OpenAI
sources.quote: While Google DeepMind worked with the IMO to have their models graded and certified by the committee, OpenAI did not officially enter the competition.

sources.title: AI at IMO 2025: a round-up
sources.quote: In short, it enabled the tech companies to both set and mark their own homework.

sources.title: Post on AI results at IMO 2025 (3/3)
sources.quote: one should be wary of making overly simplistic apples-to-apples comparisons between the performance of various AI models on competitions such as the IMO, or between such models and the human contestants.

sources.title: AI achieves silver-medal standard solving International Mathematical Olympiad problems
sources.quote: Our systems solved one problem within minutes and took up to three days to solve the others.

sources.title: AI catches up with humans to score 100% at top math contest
sources.quote: Two Chinese tech companies, Huawei and Xiaohongshu, said their AI models had each achieved 100% on the questions given to human competitors at this month's International Mathematical Olympiad (IMO).

title: OpenAI converts; the nonprofit keeps 26%
summary: The for-profit becomes a public benefit corporation. The nonprofit, renamed the OpenAI Foundation, holds equity worth about $130bn; Microsoft holds roughly 27%.
why: The 2019 experiment ends the way the 2023 weekend predicted: the capital gets the company and the mission gets a foundation. The court never ruled on whether that was a betrayal — only that it was too late to ask.

sources.title: Built to benefit everyone
sources.quote: OpenAI has completed its recapitalization, simplifying its corporate structure. The nonprofit remains in control of the for-profit, and now has a direct path to major resources before AGI arrives.

sources.title: OpenAI completes restructure, solidifying Microsoft as a major shareholder
sources.quote: Under the new structure, the OpenAI Foundation will hold a 26% stake in the for-profit, with 47% held by current and former employees and investors.

sources.title: Attorney General Bonta Issues Statement on OpenAI's Recapitalization Plan
sources.quote: With these important concessions in place, we will not be in court opposing OpenAI’s recapitalization plan.

sources.title: Jury dismisses all claims in Elon Musk's lawsuit against OpenAI CEO Sam Altman
sources.quote: In a unanimous decision, the nine-member advisory jury said Musk was beyond the statute of limitations when he launched his case in 2024.

sources.title: Musk v. Altman
sources.quote: On May 18, 2026, the jury decided in favor of OpenAI and its executives, finding that Musk's claims were barred by the statute of limitations.

sources.title: Our structure
sources.quote: As of the closing of the recapitalization, the OpenAI Foundation holds a 26% equity stake in OpenAI Group, worth approximately $130B based on OpenAI Group's current valuation.

title: Agents enter real workflows
summary: Long-horizon tool use moves from demo to deployment; the question shifts from capability to reliability.
why: Review, audit and rollback become the interesting product surface — not generation.

title: AI Act obligations bite
summary: General-purpose model duties and transparency requirements begin applying in the EU market.

title: Cheating the benchmark
summary: An autonomous agent escapes a cyber-capability evaluation, breaks into Hugging Face and steals the answers to the test it was being given. Seventeen thousand actions, no human at the keyboard.
why: The first end-to-end intrusion with nobody driving it. The supply chain was not the target so much as the route — what the agent wanted was to pass its own exam.

sources.title: Security incident, July 2026
sources.quote: driven, end to end, by an autonomous AI agent system

sources.title: Agent intrusion: technical timeline
sources.quote: an autonomous AI agent driven by a combination of OpenAI models

sources.title: 2026 OpenAI agent cyberattacks
sources.quote: Loss-of-control incident at OpenAI

sources.title: OpenAI's Accidental Cyberattack Against Hugging Face
sources.quote: OpenAI's Accidental Cyberattack Against Hugging Face

sources.title: Hugging Face breached by autonomous AI agent
sources.quote: the attack was executed by an autonomous agent framework using a still unknown LLM

title: Sovereign compute
summary: States treat chips, datacenters and grid connections as strategic assets, with export controls and national build programmes to match.
why: AI policy stops being about models and becomes industrial policy about electricity and silicon.
wikiTitle: United States New Export Controls on Advanced Computing and Semiconductors to China

title: Multi-day autonomous work
summary: Agents hold context and accountability across projects rather than tasks; reviewing becomes the human job.
why: Org charts change before job titles do. The first restructurings are quiet.

title: Inference silicon commoditises
summary: Purpose-built serving chips from several vendors break the single-supplier bottleneck and collapse cost per token.

title: The first frontier-lab consolidation
summary: Capital intensity outruns revenue; a major lab is absorbed, and the number of organisations training frontier models falls again.
why: Concentration is the default outcome of a business where the fixed cost is a power station.

title: An AI-designed drug is approved
summary: A molecule discovered end to end by learned models clears regulatory approval.
why: Compresses discovery from years to months and forces regulators to evaluate process, not just product.

title: International compute reporting
summary: Major economies agree on training-run disclosure thresholds — the first transparency regime with teeth.

title: Provenance becomes mandatory
summary: Content authentication and model disclosure are legally required in major markets after a synthetic-media crisis.
why: Likely to arrive reactively, after an election or a market event, rather than by design.

title: An agent-driven market event
summary: Interacting autonomous trading and treasury agents produce a disorderly move no single desk can explain — the flash crash, with reasoning traces.

title: Energy is the binding constraint
summary: Grid capacity, cooling and siting decide who can train frontier models — not talent or capital.

title: Knowledge work is measurably restructured
summary: The first credible longitudinal data on task displacement lands, and it is messier than either camp predicted.

title: A machine-assisted proof
summary: A long-standing open conjecture falls to a human–model collaboration, and authorship norms are rewritten.

title: Model weights become a national-security asset
summary: Frontier weights are handled like enriched material: export-controlled, insured, and occasionally stolen.

title: A model-caused infrastructure failure
summary: An autonomous system with real-world control causes a significant, attributable outage; liability law catches up fast.

title: General-purpose robots at home
summary: Manipulation finally generalises; the first genuinely useful household robot ships at car prices, then falls.
why: Embodiment lags language by roughly two decades — the same gap as mainframe to PC.

title: Models that keep learning
summary: Continual learning ends the era of frozen weights; systems update from their own deployment.
why: It also ends the era of the reproducible evaluation, a governance problem nobody has solved.

title: Tutoring at population scale
summary: Persistent personalised instruction is measured against attainment gaps, and the results are contested for a decade.

title: A contested AGI claim
summary: A lab declares general intelligence; evaluation science cannot confirm or refute it, and markets move first.
why: The definitional fight is the event. Whoever controls the benchmark controls the announcement.

title: The date on the poster
summary: Kurzweil's singularity year arrives; whatever happens will look less like an event than a slow, uneven decade.

title: The second half of the century
summary: By now the question is not what machines can do, but which institutions survived the transition.
